studies.title: A Man From Among Them
studies.meaning: Three disconnected letters open the surah, followed by a claim about the Book they head. Then comes a question about astonishment. The objection was never that God might speak, but that He spoke through a neighbour. Commentators read the promise of a sure footing as reward already secured, as honest precedence with God, or as firm standing ahead of the believers. The charge of sorcery concedes the power of the words while refusing their source.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a stage when the message had been public long enough for the city to settle into a position on it. Curiosity had hardened into accusation. This surah belongs to a small group that open with the same three letters and then speak immediately about scripture. Its audience knew the speaker personally, had traded with him, and had once trusted him with their deposits.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to restrain and to judge soundly. Applied to a book it carries both wisdom of content and tightness of construction, something whose parts hold and cannot be pulled loose.
Literally a foot of truthfulness. The classical range covers a reward already stored up, an honest standing with God, and firm ground underfoot. The image is of standing, not of receiving.
The accusation admits that the words worked. Sorcery was the available account of speech that moved crowds and divided households, and the same charge was thrown at earlier messengers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on reputation. A man's word was collateral on a caravan loan, and every household knew who honoured his and who did not. That is exactly where the objection landed: not on the content of the message but on the ordinariness of the man carrying it. Someone who had grown up in your alleys, whose uncles you could name, was the last person you expected speech from beyond to arrive through.
studies.didYouKnow: These three letters head exactly five surahs of the Quran: the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, fourteenth and fifteenth. The thirteenth interrupts the run by adding a fourth letter. In every one of the five, the letters are followed immediately by a statement about the Book, and nowhere in the text is any explanation of the letters themselves given.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The difficulty of revelation is located in the messenger, not the message. Speaking through someone embedded in a community means the words arrive with a biography attached and can be argued with on those grounds. The demand for something more impressive is a request to be spared the work of weighing content. Notice that the good news is announced before any argument is offered.

crossReferences.why: States the objection directly: what stopped people believing was that God sent a human messenger.
The same complaint in detail, that this messenger eats food and walks through the markets.
Records both halves of the reaction here, astonishment at a warner from among them, then the charge of magic.

studies.applyIt: Notice today the moment you dismiss something true because of who said it. A colleague you find tiresome, a relative you filed away years ago. Try holding the sentence on its own for ten seconds before you attach it to the person. Familiarity did work in Mecca that argument could not, and it still does.

studies.title: Governing All Things
studies.meaning: Four claims arrive in one sentence: God made the heavens and the earth over six days, rose above the Throne, runs the affair continuously, and admits no intercessor without leave. Classical commentators treat the settling over the Throne as affirmed without asking how, and they read the present-tense governing as the answer to a suspicion that a creator might finish and withdraw. The conclusion drawn is worship, and the closing question asks only for reflection.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience already accepted a supreme creator; what they disputed was whether He was reachable without go-betweens. Their shrine housed images understood as advocates who could carry a petition upward. Placing intercession entirely under permission cuts at that arrangement without denying that intercession exists. The surah returns to the same point several times before it is finished.

keyTerms.note: The commentators affirm the word without assigning it a manner, and warn against picturing a body seated. What it establishes is completed sovereignty over creation rather than any location within it.
From a root meaning to consider the outcome of a matter. The form is continuous, so it describes ongoing administration with an end in view, not a single act of setting things going.
One who joins his petition to another's, from a root meaning to make even-numbered. The word is not denied here; it is placed downstream of permission, which relocates the whole transaction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Access in Mecca ran through patrons. A stranger entering the city sought protection from a man of standing before he could trade safely, and a debtor in trouble looked for someone to speak on his behalf to the creditor. Everyone understood that reaching a powerful person meant finding someone he already listened to. That instinct was carried straight into worship, which is what this ayah addresses.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that God created the heavens and the earth in six days appears seven times in the Quran, and in five of those places it is followed immediately by the settling over the Throne. Nowhere is the length of a day here defined, and the classical commentators declined to fix it, noting only that the sun was not yet made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation and government are held together, so the world is not left running on its own momentum. Sovereignty is described in a way that resists imagining, and the tradition guards that carefully. Most consequential is what happens to intercession: it is neither abolished nor made a lever, but folded inside permission, so hope survives while the idea of pressuring God does not.

crossReferences.why: The same six days and Throne, expanded into night pursuing day and the stars under command.
Puts intercession under permission in the same terms, inside the best-known description of God.
Repeats the sequence and adds that apart from Him you have no master and no intercessor.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing today that is running without you: traffic lights, the person who restocks your shop, your own heartbeat. Follow it back a step or two and notice how little of it you arranged. The ayah does not ask you to feel small. It asks you to reflect, which is slower and more interesting.

studies.title: He Begins It And Repeats It
studies.meaning: The argument for resurrection here is not a threat but a comparison. Whoever started a thing can start it again, and the second time is not harder than the first. That reasoning is offered as a promise God has bound Himself to, described as true rather than likely. What follows is a split outcome, and the wording is careful: the reward is given with equity, while the punishment is tied precisely to what people persisted in.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Bodily resurrection was the point at which many listeners stopped, not the existence of God. Bones in the ground looked like the end of an argument, and the objection is quoted elsewhere in exactly those words. The surah answers it early and then leaves it, returning through story and sign rather than repeating the proof.

keyTerms.note: The verb for starting something with no model in front of you. Placing it beside the verb for repeating turns resurrection into the easier of the two acts, which is the whole force of the sentence.
Fairness as a settled share rather than as a feeling. Attached to reward, it rules out favouritism, and the classical readings note that God's generosity operates above the measure, never below it.
Water heated to its limit. The same root gives words for a close relative and for a fever, so the term carries nearness and heat together, which is why the image is drinking rather than burning.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was the measure of everything in that landscape. A caravan planned its stages by wells, a household's standing showed in what it could offer a guest to drink, and cool water was the first courtesy extended at a door. Boiling water as the drink set before a person inverts the deepest form of Arabian hospitality, which is why the image needed no explanation to its first hearers.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of originating creation with repeating it recurs across the Quran as a compact argument, and this surah uses it twice within thirty-one verses, the second time as a challenge to name any partner who can do the same. Both occurrences keep the two verbs adjacent, so the second act is always heard as an echo of the first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Resurrection is presented as a matter of consistency rather than of power alone. If the return is real, then the moral weight of a life does not evaporate with the body, and justice is not confined to what courts can reach. The passage also binds God by His own promise, which is a striking move: the certainty offered to the reader rests on God's truthfulness, not on the reader's imagination.

crossReferences.why: States the same argument as a principle, that repeating creation is easier for God than beginning it.
Answers the objection about decayed bones with the one who gave them life the first time.
Turns this pair of verbs into a direct question about whether any partner can do the same.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you rebuilt once: a friendship, a routine, a room after a move. Recall how the second attempt went compared with the first. You already know from small things that starting over is not the same as starting cold. Let that be what you carry into the next hard beginning you face this week.

studies.title: Stations For The Moon
studies.meaning: Two lights are named with two different words, and the difference is deliberate: one blazes, the other is a milder illumination. Then the moon is given measured stations, and a purpose is attached to the measuring, which is that people can count years and keep accounts. The passage treats the sky as an instrument as much as an ornament. It closes by saying none of this was made idly, and that the signs are set out in detail for those who will actually learn.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Arabia lived by a lunar calendar, and the sacred months that made pilgrimage and trade possible were fixed by the moon's cycle. Sky-watching was ordinary competence, not specialist knowledge. The surah is arguing that the same regularity everyone relied on for business is itself an argument, and that people who read the sky for profit might read it for meaning.

keyTerms.note: Light that a thing gives off from itself, with heat implied. Classical commentators noticed that the sun receives this word while the moon receives a gentler one, and treated the pairing as intentional.
The general word for light that lets things be seen. Al-Tabari and others read the contrast with the sun's word as marking a difference in kind, not merely in brightness.
The word for the halting places a traveller stops at on a route. Applied to the moon it turns the month into a journey with named stages, which is how Arabian navigators used it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan leaving Mecca timed its departure by the moon and steered at night by stars whose rising positions men had memorised as children. Debts fell due at the new crescent, and the truce months that let rival tribes trade at the fairs began and ended by the same sighting. Nobody in that audience needed the ayah explained; they needed the ordinary sky pointed at.
studies.didYouKnow: The stations of the moon were a working system in pre-Islamic Arabia, twenty-eight recognised positions used to track the year and predict rain. The word this ayah uses is the same one those observers used. Elsewhere the Quran calls the crescents timetables for people, again defining the sky by what it lets human beings organise.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Order in creation is given a purpose that includes the human being. The heavens are not simply large and impressive; they are calibrated, and the calibration is described as being for you. That joins two claims that often drift apart: that the universe is made with truth, and that it is made habitable. Knowledge, in this framing, is not opposed to wonder but is the form wonder takes.

crossReferences.why: Gives night and day the same double purpose, seeking provision and knowing the count of years.
Answers a question about the moon's phases by calling them timetables for people and pilgrimage.
Pairs the breaking of dawn with sun and moon set for calculation, ending on the same two names.

studies.applyIt: Find the moon tonight and note which shape it is. Then check it again in three days. Doing this twice is enough to feel the difference between knowing the moon has phases and watching one. The ayah connects counting to attention; most of us have the counting outsourced and have lost the watching.

studies.title: Signs For The Watchful
studies.meaning: A single short sentence gathers everything: the turning of night into day, and whatever God has made anywhere in the heavens and the earth. Both are called signs. The qualification at the end is the interesting part, because the signs are said to be there for people who keep a certain wariness before God, not for people who are clever. Commentators read this as saying the evidence is public while the capacity to be moved by it is a moral condition rather than an intellectual one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This ayah closes a short sequence that began with creation and the Throne and moved through sun and moon. The surah is building an argument from what its audience already granted, before turning to what they denied. No specific occasion is reported for it; the setting is the general one of a city that acknowledged a creator and drew none of the conclusions.

keyTerms.note: The noun covers both difference and taking turns, from a root meaning to come after. Applied to night and day it names the handover itself, not the two states, which is where the regularity shows.
The same word used for verses of scripture. Using it for the sky puts creation and revelation in one category, two texts pointing the same direction, and the Quran keeps the overlap deliberately.
From a root meaning to take a shield. It describes a wariness that keeps a person from crossing certain lines, and the ayah makes that posture the condition for seeing what is plainly there.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a desert climate the changeover between night and day is not gradual; heat drops fast after sunset and the stars arrive quickly. Travel was arranged around it, with the hardest stages walked in darkness and rest taken through the worst of the sun. The alternation this ayah points at was a daily negotiation for its first hearers, something their bodies tracked without instruments.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses one word for a verse of scripture and for a feature of the natural world, and this ayah applies it to the sky. The pattern of closing such passages with a clause naming who benefits runs through this whole opening section, and each clause names a different group: people who know, people who are watchful, people who reflect.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Evidence is not treated here as neutral. The same sunrise stands in front of everyone, and the passage says only some read it, which locates the difference inside the observer. That resists two errors at once: the claim that proof compels belief, and the claim that faith has nothing to do with what can be seen. Attention is presented as the moral act, and the signs remain available for anyone who takes it up.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about night and day, naming people of understanding as the ones who see.
Expands the same list across winds, rain, ships and animals, all called signs for those who reason.
Runs the same catalogue three times, each time closing with a different qualifying clause.

studies.applyIt: Watch one sunset this week from beginning to end without a screen in your hand. It takes about twenty minutes. Do not try to feel anything in particular. The ayah does not ask for emotion, it asks for the kind of attention that most of us have quietly stopped paying to things that happen every single day.

studies.title: Content And At Ease
studies.meaning: No argument is denied here and no doctrine is stated. What is described is a settling: not expecting to meet God, being satisfied with this life, and growing comfortable inside it. Alongside that runs an inattention to the signs. Commentators note that the wording targets a way of living rather than a stated position, so a person could hold the right beliefs and still answer this description. The outcome named uses the word for shelter, which turns the sentence bitter.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to an audience with a great deal to lose. The city's leading families were prosperous, their trade routes were secure, and the arrangement suited them. A message that made this life provisional threatened the settlement itself. The passage follows immediately on three ayat about signs in the sky and earth, so the heedlessness it names is heedlessness of something just placed in front of the reader.

keyTerms.note: From a root for level ground and a calmed heart. The word is usually warm in the Quran; used here of the present life it names a peace that has attached itself to the wrong thing.
Not ignorance but inattention. The root describes leaving something unattended rather than never having known it, so the charge is about where the eyes rest, not about missing information.
The place a traveller turns aside to for shelter, the same word used for the shade a herd gathers in. Applying it to the Fire makes what was sought as safety into the destination.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca had no farmland and no river. Its wealth came entirely from managing a shrine and a trade corridor, which meant its prosperity was an achievement people could feel they had built. A merchant with two caravan seasons behind him and a house near the sanctuary had every reason to call his position settled. That satisfaction is the specific thing this passage names, not poverty and not luxury.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for growing settled and at rest appears elsewhere in the Quran for hearts finding rest in the remembrance of God, and for a soul addressed as tranquil at the point of return. The same root that describes the deepest peace available to a person is used here for the shallowest, and only the object attached to it changes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates unbelief in the direction of a life rather than in a proposition. What is criticised is not enjoying the world but taking it as final, treating the visible as the whole account. That leaves ordinary comfort untouched while questioning what a person rests their weight on. It also implies that expectation shapes conduct: what you take to be coming determines what you find worth doing now.

crossReferences.why: States the same preference plainly, that people choose the present life though the next is better and lasting.
Uses the same verb for hearts growing settled, but attached to the remembrance of God instead.
Draws the contrast in terms of provision, what you are given now against what God keeps.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you would be most reluctant to lose, and be honest rather than pious about the answer. Then notice how much of this week was arranged around protecting it. The passage is not asking you to give it up. It is asking whether you have quietly begun treating it as the point of the whole thing.

studies.title: Guided By Their Faith
studies.meaning: The short phrase in the middle carries the weight: their Lord guides them by their faith. Commentators divide over what it points to. Some read it as guidance in this life given in proportion to belief already held, so that acting on what you know earns more to act on. Others read it as light on the Day of return, faith itself becoming the thing that shows the way forward. Both readings agree that guidance is not a single event but something that accumulates.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, placed directly against the description that precedes it. The surah has just named people who settled into this life and stopped noticing; this ayah names the opposite case in the same grammatical shape, beginning with the same words. Reading them as a pair is how the classical commentators handle the passage, since neither sentence explains itself alone.

keyTerms.note: From a root for showing the road and for a gift. The verb is continuous, which is why the commentators read it as ongoing direction rather than an initial rescue from error.
The attached particle can mean because of or by means of, and the tradition preserves both. Faith is either the reason guidance is given or the instrument through which it is walked.
From a root meaning softness and comfort, the opposite of hardship rather than of poverty. It names the quality of the gardens, not their contents, so the phrase describes a condition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guides were hired, not borrowed. A merchant crossing to Syria paid a man who knew where the wells sat and which route was passable that season, and following him closely was the difference between arriving and not. Everyone understood that a guide is only useful to someone already walking. The image of rivers running underneath was equally concrete to people whose water came up from wells by rope.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of six places where the Quran names the Gardens of Bliss, and the only one that ties entry to being guided by faith rather than to deeds alone. Across the Quran the picture of rivers running beneath is the most frequent single image of the garden, repeated far more often than any description of what grows there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as responsive. It comes to those who already believe, which makes belief a beginning rather than a finish line, and rules out treating direction from God as a one-time delivery. The passage also links inner state to final destination without making the connection mechanical: what is promised is a place, but the road to it runs through what the person already holds and keeps acting on.

crossReferences.why: Says the same thing in different words: those who are guided, He increases in guidance.
Attaches guidance of the heart to belief in a moment of disaster, the practical form of this promise.
Shows faith becoming visible light running ahead of believers on the Day of return.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you already know is right and have not been doing, and do it once today. Small is better. The ayah describes guidance arriving through faith rather than before it, and the ordinary experience matches: clarity about the next step usually shows up after you take the one you were avoiding.

studies.title: The Last Of Their Call
studies.meaning: The whole speech of the garden is given in one line, and it has three parts. It opens by declaring God free of every defect, it passes sideways into a greeting exchanged between people, and it closes on praise. What is missing is asking. The word used for their call normally introduces a request, and here it contains none, which the commentators read as the sign that nothing is left wanting. Worship continues after need has ended.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a short passage that has just set two ways of living side by side. The surah is describing outcomes rather than reporting an occasion. Its first hearers already knew what a life of petition sounded like, since prayer at the sanctuary was largely a matter of asking for rain, safe passage and offspring, and the picture drawn here removes exactly that element.

keyTerms.note: From the root for summoning and for supplication, the same one behind the ordinary word for prayer of request. Its use for speech containing no request is what gives the ayah its point.

A declaration that God is far removed from any deficiency, built on a root suggesting swimming or moving freely away. It clears ground rather than describing, denying limits before anything is affirmed.
From a root meaning life, so a greeting is literally a wish that the other live. That the greeting exchanged is peace makes the social air of the place part of its description.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Greeting was serious business in a tribal society. The words exchanged when two parties met on a road announced whether this was an encounter or a threat, and travellers rehearsed them. A wrong greeting could start something. Peace as the standing word in the garden would have registered first as the removal of that whole calculation, an entire category of vigilance switched off.
studies.didYouKnow: The final words placed in the mouths of the people of the garden are the same words that open the Quran's first surah, praise to God, Lord of the Worlds. Classical commentators noticed the loop: the Book begins where the destination ends. The greeting named in the middle also becomes the greeting of the community in this life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Worship is shown to outlast its usual motives. If praise continues where there is no danger, no shortage and nothing to request, then it was never only a transaction, and the reward turns out to include the very thing that was asked of people. The order also matters: God is glorified first, peace passes between people second, and gratitude comes last, as a response rather than a prompt.

crossReferences.why: The Quran opens with the exact words this ayah gives as the last speech of the garden.
Names the same greeting of peace as what those admitted to the gardens say to each other.
Shows praise arriving as the first response once sorrow has been lifted away entirely.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your talking to God this week was a request. Not to criticise it, since asking is invited elsewhere in the Book. Just add one sentence at the end of a prayer that asks for nothing at all. Say it after the request, in the order this ayah uses, and see whether it changes the shape of the whole.

studies.title: If Harm Came As Fast
studies.meaning: A conditional sentence measures one thing against another. People press for good to arrive quickly; suppose harm were delivered at that same speed. The classical commentators take this in two ways, either of the curses people utter in anger, or of the punishment sceptics dared God to send. Under either reading the answer is the same: their appointed span would already be over. What follows is not comfort. Being left to wander in one's own excess is described as a consequence, not a reprieve.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some in the city had openly challenged God to rain stones on them if the message were true, a demand the Quran records elsewhere in their own words. The passage answers a taunt without answering it on its terms. Every delay they read as proof of nothing happening is presented instead as a term still running.

keyTerms.note: The root carries both speed and impatience, and the Quran uses it elsewhere to say the human being was made of haste. Here the same verb is applied first to God, then to people.
A fixed period with a known end, the word used for the due date of a debt. It names a length of time rather than a moment, so what is finished is a span, not an event.
From a root describing water that rises past its banks. It pictures wrongdoing as overflow rather than as trespass, something that spreads by its own pressure once nothing checks it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cursing was ordinary speech. A man who lost a camel or quarrelled with a cousin would call ruin down on him in front of witnesses, and poets built reputations on elaborate imprecations against rival tribes. Nobody expected these to be enforced. A world where every angry sentence took effect the moment it was spoken would have emptied the peninsula within a season, and the first hearers knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah belongs to a small group that make the same argument by supposing God acted immediately. Two of them state that if He seized people for what they had earned, not one living creature would be left on the earth's surface. In each case the sentence is built as an unreal condition, so the delay is presented as the actual state of affairs rather than as a concession.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forbearance is shown as a deliberate withholding, which makes ordinary time itself a gift rather than a neutral background. The passage also declines to treat unanswered defiance as evidence either way. Most seriously, it describes a form of being left alone that is worse than being stopped: when nothing interrupts a person, the wandering continues, and the absence of a check turns out to be its own kind of verdict.

crossReferences.why: States the human tendency exactly, praying for evil as one prays for good, out of haste.
Makes the same unreal condition explicit, that immediate reckoning would leave nothing alive.
Records the taunt this ayah answers, a demand that stones be rained down from the sky.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you asked for in anger and did not get. A confrontation you wanted, a message you nearly sent, a wish about someone who had wronged you. Most people have at least one they are now relieved about. Let that be the concrete form of this ayah rather than an idea, and notice what the delay did for you.

studies.title: Lying, Sitting, Standing
studies.meaning: Three postures are listed in a rising order, and the commentators read them as covering every condition a person can pray from, starting with the one who cannot get up. That is how thoroughly trouble produces prayer. Then relief arrives and the man walks on, and the comparison is exact: as if he had never called at all. The closing clause widens the case, saying that this is how conduct comes to look acceptable to those who go past limits.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to an audience whose religion was largely transactional. Petitions were made at the sanctuary in emergencies and vows were paid when the emergency passed. The passage does not report a particular incident. It describes a pattern the surah will return to twice more, once at sea in a storm and once after relief from hardship, each time with the same shape and different scenery.

keyTerms.note: Damage that reaches a person's body or livelihood, distinguished from harm someone does to another. The word appears twice in this ayah, once as what arrives and once as what is lifted.
A plain verb of movement, not of denial or rebellion. The choice is deliberate: nothing dramatic happens, the man simply continues on his way, which is what makes the picture recognisable.
From a root for exceeding a proper measure, used of spending and of conduct alike. It names people who have lost a sense of proportion rather than people committing one identifiable offence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Illness in that world was largely waited out. There were bonesetters, cauterisation and remedies of honey and herbs, but for a fever the household could do little except keep the sick person cool and watch. Long hours flat on a mat with nothing to do but ask were the ordinary experience of being unwell, and the ayah begins from precisely that position before working upward.
studies.didYouKnow: The same three postures appear elsewhere in the Quran in the reverse order, standing, sitting and lying on their sides, describing people who remember God in every condition. Read together, the two lists use one set of bodily positions to mark opposite habits: one group prays through all of them only under pressure, the other through all of them regardless.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats forgetfulness rather than denial as the characteristic human failure. Nothing is argued and nothing is renounced; a man simply resumes. That is a more uncomfortable diagnosis than rebellion, because it does not require a decision. It also implies that crisis reveals something true about a person, since the prayer offered flat on one's back was not insincere, only unsupported by anything once the pressure lifted.

crossReferences.why: Gives the identical sequence with the added detail that he forgets what he had been praying for.
Reverses the order to show the same man withdrawing in comfort and praying at length in trouble.
Uses the same three postures for those who remember God continuously, not only under pressure.

studies.applyIt: Remember something you badly wanted and eventually received. Go back and find what you promised while you were waiting. Then check honestly whether you kept it. If you did not, pick one small piece of that promise and do it this week, without telling anyone. That is the ayah's whole subject, handled at the scale you can actually reach.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: To See How You Behave
studies.meaning: Two sentences run a whole history in miniature. Earlier peoples were removed once wrongdoing was established and evidence had reached them, and the sequence is stated carefully: the messengers came first. Then the address turns to the listeners themselves, who are told they occupy the ground the earlier ones vacated. The clause about seeing how you behave is read by the commentators as bringing into the open what God already knows, so that the record is made rather than discovered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Trade caravans from Mecca passed abandoned settlements on both the northern and southern routes, and the Quran elsewhere tells its audience that they walk by such places morning and evening. The argument works because the ruins were part of ordinary geography. Nothing in the passage points to one occasion; it appeals to a landscape the merchants of the city crossed every season.

keyTerms.note: The word means both a generation of people and the span they occupy. Scholars differ on the length intended, giving figures from forty years upward, and none of the classical readings insists on a number.
Plural of the word for one who comes after and takes another's place. It carries no honour by itself, only the fact of standing where someone else stood and inheriting the same conditions.
A verb of looking, not of finding out. The commentators explain it as knowledge becoming visible in events, so that conduct is produced and witnessed rather than predicted from the outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The peninsula was full of the leftovers of people who had done better than the current occupants. Carved facades stood in the rock north of Medina, dams and irrigation channels lay broken in the south, and place names preserved tribes that no longer existed. A merchant could water his camels at a well dug by a vanished people. Succession was not an abstraction; it was where you camped.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about being made successors so that God may see how you behave appears in almost identical words in another surah, spoken by Moses to Israelites who were being persecuted and were promised the land of their oppressors. In both places the promise of inheritance arrives with the same condition attached, which turns a reward into an assignment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Inheritance is presented as a test rather than a verdict. Occupying a place proves nothing about deserving it, since the previous occupants also held it and were removed. That undercuts the assumption that success is endorsement, and it puts every generation in the same position as the last. The mention of messengers arriving first also establishes that no removal is described as happening before the case was made.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the same wording, promising succession in the land and then watching how people act.
Names the same role of successors and states directly that the differences between people are a test.
Points to earlier generations whose dwellings the audience physically walks through, as signs.

studies.applyIt: Find out who lived in your home before you did. A neighbour will often know, or the deeds will. Hold that for a moment: someone measured these rooms, argued in them, and left. You are the current occupant of a place that has had others and will have more. That is the ayah's exact posture, at the smallest scale available.

studies.title: Bring Another Or Change It
studies.meaning: The request comes in two versions, a different recitation altogether or an edited one, and commentators note that what the objectors wanted removed were the passages against their images. The reply refuses on grounds of position rather than preference: the one reciting has no authority to revise what he did not compose. Then the answer turns personal. He says he is afraid of a great Day if he disobeys, which is an odd thing for a man inventing a religion to say about himself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Negotiation was the city's normal instrument, and the leadership had already tried offers of wealth and status. This is the same approach applied to the text: keep the message but drop the clauses that cost us. Reports of such approaches are widely transmitted in the classical sources, though they are attached to the period generally rather than to a single meeting.

keyTerms.note: The verb for swapping one thing for another, not for correcting an error. What was asked was a replacement of particular passages, which is why the answer speaks about authority rather than about accuracy.
Literally from the direction of myself. The phrase locates the source of speech, and by denying that source it separates the man from the words in the plainest terms available.
A passive form of a verb for swift, hidden communication. Keeping it passive leaves the speaker as recipient throughout the sentence, with no grammatical room to be the author.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Poetry was the prestige art of Arabia, and poets revised constantly. A famous ode might be reworked over a season before the fair at Ukaz, and audiences knew that a line could be improved, sold, or tailored to a patron who was paying. Against that background the request was entirely reasonable. It assumed the ordinary relationship between a composer and his material.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb the objectors use for changing the text appears again in this same surah, forty-nine verses later, in the statement that there is no altering the words of God. The demand and its answer are built on one root, so the surah refuses the request twice: once in the reply given to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and once as a plain fact about the words themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is defined by what the recipient cannot do with it. A messenger who could adjust the message would be its author, and the whole category would collapse into authorship. The passage also makes fear part of the evidence, since the person best placed to know whether the words were his own is the one most afraid of tampering with them. Obedience here is presented as constraint, not as privilege.

crossReferences.why: States the consequence in the strongest terms if the messenger had attributed any words to God himself.
Answers the demand later in this surah, saying there is no alteration to the words of God.
Describes the pressure to invent something else against God, and how close it came to working.

studies.applyIt: Think of a text you are bound by and cannot edit: a contract, a diagnosis, a message from someone who has died. Notice how differently you read something you are not permitted to adjust. Then read a page of the Quran today with that same posture, resisting the small internal edits we all make to soften what we would rather it said.

studies.title: The Home Of Peace
studies.meaning: Two motions are described and they are not the same. God calls to the Home of Peace, and He guides whom He wills to a straight path, so an open invitation and a particular guiding stand together in one sentence. The commentators keep both without dissolving the tension. Then the reward: goodness, and something extra which is left unnamed. The explanation most often given for the addition is the sight of God, though the ayah says only more.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah largely occupied with people who wanted a different kind of sign and who treated this life as the whole account. The passage arrives just after a parable comparing worldly life to vegetation that flourishes and is cut down overnight. The commentators read the invitation as the answer to that parable, and record no specific occasion for the ayat themselves.

keyTerms.note: The word for a dwelling with a courtyard, a household rather than a building. Joined to a word for wholeness and safety, it names the destination as a place to live in rather than a state to reach.
A plain word for addition, left without an object. The commentators most often explain it as the sight of God, and note that the ayah deliberately leaves the extra unspecified.
A film of dust or smoke settling on something, the darkening that comes over a face at bad news. Denying it is a physical description, since the face is where humiliation shows first.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Faces were read constantly in that society. A man returning from a failed negotiation, a family that had lost a claim, a debtor passing his creditor: everyone knew the news before anybody spoke. Poetry describes the dust of humiliation settling on a man's features. Promising that neither dust nor lowliness would touch these faces spoke to a culture where standing was worn openly.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the phrase Home of Peace only twice, here and at 6:127, and in both places it is paired with a statement about God's relation to those who receive it. The word for peace inside it is the same one used as the greeting exchanged there, so the destination is named after what is said inside it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The invitation is universal and the guidance is particular, and the passage sets them side by side without softening either. Classical discussion has kept both, treating the call as genuinely addressed to everyone while the arrival is not in human hands alone. The reward then refuses to be measured: goodness is matched to what was done, and something further is added with no stated equivalent.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same name for the destination, adding that He is their ally.
Precedes it with the parable of vegetation cut down that this invitation answers.
States the principle of matching, that the reward of good is nothing but good.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often the word peace passes your lips today as a greeting, and let one of those be deliberate. The destination in this ayah is named after that word. It costs nothing to mean it once, and the passage suggests the greeting and the address are the same thing at different distances.

studies.title: Healing For What Is Inside
studies.meaning: Four things are named and the address narrows as it goes. Counsel arrives for all people, then healing for what is in the chests, then guidance and mercy, and these last two are specified for believers. The commentators note that healing is placed before guidance, so the text is described as treating something before it teaches anything. The following ayah then tells people what to be glad about, and weighs it against what they accumulate.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is largely addressed to an audience arguing about where the revelation came from, and this passage steps outside that argument to describe what the text does instead. The commentators record no specific occasion, and read the address to all people as a deliberate widening after a long stretch aimed at opponents.

keyTerms.note: Speech aimed at softening rather than informing, the kind that works on the will. Naming it first places the text's effect before its content, which the sequence of the ayah then continues.
The ordinary medical word for recovery from illness. Its object here is what is in the chests, so the trouble being treated is located inside a person rather than in their circumstances.
The Quran uses this for the seat of what a person conceals: doubt, resentment, intention. Naming the chest rather than the heart points at the container rather than at the organ inside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medicine in Arabia was practical and limited: cautery, cupping, honey, herbs, and the setting of bones. Illnesses of the chest were understood physically, and the vocabulary of cure was familiar to everyone. Using that word for what a recitation does to a person's inner state borrowed language from a craft the audience trusted, and applied it to something nobody could see.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes itself as healing in several places, and the descriptions always carry a limit. One passage calls it healing and mercy for believers while adding nothing but loss for wrongdoers; another calls it guidance and healing for those who believe and something quite different for those who do not.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is presented as treatment before instruction, which assumes a particular diagnosis: the obstacle to guidance is not a lack of information but something lodged inside a person. That explains how the same text can be read by two people with opposite results. The following ayah then relocates joy, moving it from what has been gathered to what has been given, and it does so by command rather than by argument.

crossReferences.why: Calls the revelation healing and mercy for believers, and loss for wrongdoers.
Describes it as guidance and healing for some and as deafness for others.
Names the remembrance of God as what settles hearts, describing the same effect.

studies.applyIt: Pick one passage you find difficult, and instead of asking what it teaches, ask what it disturbs. Sit with the discomfort for a minute rather than resolving it. The ayah puts healing before guidance, and treatment usually feels worse than instruction before it starts feeling better.

studies.title: The Friends Of God
studies.meaning: An attention marker opens the passage, the particle used to announce something. Then a claim about the allies of God, followed by a definition that is deliberately plain: those who believed and used to guard themselves. No rank, no title, no separate class. Good news is promised in this life as well as the next, and the words are said to be unalterable. The last ayah turns to the messenger and tells him not to be saddened by talk.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressing people who claimed intermediaries and privileged access. The definition given here is read by the commentators as answering that: the category of God's allies is fixed by two ordinary qualities available to anybody. Classical sources record several explanations of the good news promised in this life, including true dreams, and preserve the range without settling it.

keyTerms.note: From a root for nearness and for taking charge of someone. The word describes a two-sided closeness, which is why the same term is used of God towards believers elsewhere in the Quran.
From a root for skin and for the face brightening at news. The word names the physical effect of good news, so what is promised includes something felt rather than only something learned.
Strength that cannot be reached or reduced, the quality that made a fortified place impregnable. Saying that all of it belongs to God removes the standing the speakers were relying on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Holy men in Arabia held a recognised social role. Diviners, keepers of shrines and men credited with contact with the unseen were consulted, paid, and treated as a class apart. A definition of God's friends that named only belief and self-restraint, with no rite, lineage or shrine attached, cut across an established profession and the fees that came with it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase promising no fear and no grief recurs through the Quran, always in the same shape, and here it is attached not to a named community but to a category defined in the ayah that follows. Classical commentators treat the two ayat as a single sentence for that reason, since the claim would otherwise be left without a subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Closeness to God is described as available rather than allocated, and the definition given is short enough to check yourself against. The good news promised in this life keeps the passage from being wholly postponed, without specifying what it consists of, which the commentators leave open. The instruction at the end then reframes opposition: what people say is answered by a statement about where power sits.

crossReferences.why: Names God as the ally of those who believe, the other side of the word used here.
Describes angels descending on those who stayed upright with the same reassurance.
States that all honour belongs to God, answering those who seek it elsewhere.

studies.applyIt: Check yourself against the definition rather than against an ideal. Two things are named, believing and guarding yourself, and neither requires a title. If the phrase friends of God has always sounded to you like a description of somebody else, notice that the passage spends its next line making sure it is not.

studies.title: Nothing Can Turn It Back
studies.meaning: The two halves are not built the same way, and the difference is the point. Harm is described as a touch, with its removal denied to anyone but Him. Good is described as something He intends for you, with nothing able to turn His bounty back. The second clause moves from contact to purpose, and the commentators note that the asymmetry runs in favour of the good. The closing names are forgiveness and mercy rather than power.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in the closing passage of a surah that has spent its length on people calling upon things that could neither harm nor help them. The ayat before it gather the whole argument into an instruction about which way to turn. This is the final piece of that summary, and the commentators read the two divine names at the end as the surah's chosen resting point.

keyTerms.note: An agent noun from the verb to send something back. It pictures bounty as already in motion, so refusing it would mean intercepting something on its way rather than preventing a decision.

keyTerms.gloss: intends for you, wants for you
keyTerms.note: A verb of will rather than of contact. Set opposite the word for touching in the first half, it gives the good a source in intention while the harm is described only as arriving.
A general word for damage of any kind. Its indefinite form leaves the scale unspecified, so the sentence covers a minor setback and a catastrophe in exactly the same terms.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Intercession with the powerful was how anything got done. A man in trouble found someone with standing to speak for him, and a favour granted could be blocked by a rival with better access. Everyone understood that gifts could be intercepted on the way. Saying that nothing turns back this bounty described a channel with nobody standing in it, which was a strange idea in a world of brokers.
studies.didYouKnow: The first half of this ayah appears almost word for word earlier in the Quran, at 6:17, but the second half differs. There the good is a touch, matching the harm; here it is something intended, and the closing divine names change along with it. The variation is small enough to vanish in translation and consistent in the Arabic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are established at once, and they pull in different directions unless read carefully. Nothing reaches a person outside God's decree, and nothing can obstruct what He intends for them. The first removes the illusion of independent threats; the second removes the fear of blocked good. Ending on forgiveness and mercy rather than on might tells the reader which of the two the passage expects them to need.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same statement with its second half built differently, in a Meccan surah.
States that whatever mercy God opens for people, nobody can withhold it.
Asks whether the things called upon beside God could hold back His mercy.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good thing you have stopped hoping for because of who is standing in the way: a person, a system, a decision that went against you. Say the second half of this ayah about that specific case. You are not predicting an outcome. You are checking whether you had quietly promoted an obstacle into a decider.
